stories.topic: Wrong About Everything He 'Knew' About Podcasting
stories.summary: The Seen and the Unseen began seven years ago as an experiment. Amit assumed attention spans were short: grab listeners in the first fifteen seconds and keep episodes to fifteen or twenty minutes. The show went the other way. Short episodes became three- and four-hour deep dives into subjects, then seven- and eight-hour oral histories of people. The longer it got, the more love it received. His conservative estimate is twenty million hours of listening. Thirteen of the last seventeen times he was at an airport, someone stopped him to thank him. The YouTube version brings in under one percent of listens.
stories.insight: Conventional wisdom about a new medium is often carried over from old media. Amit's audience showed him that what they wanted was depth, not brevity.
stories.quote: And as it got longer and longer, I got more and more love from people.

stories.topic: Krish Ashok's Colleague Who Listens at 6x
stories.summary: Amit listens to most things at 2x and goes up to 3x when researching an episode. He raises the speed in steps so that each one starts to feel normal. On an episode of The Seen and the Unseen, Krish Ashok told him about a blind colleague who listens at 6x, a speed at which audio becomes mush for Amit.
stories.insight: The brain adapts to listening speed far more than we assume. Pauses speed up along with the words, so nuance survives. The speed that feels comfortable to you is simply where you stopped pushing.
stories.quote: Now you see the plasticity of the brain. If I take anything to 6X, beyond the point it's mush, I can't make it out. But the brain adjusts.

stories.topic: The Listener Who Interrupted a Recording
stories.summary: After hearing Amit's episode with Abhinandan Sekhri, a listener told Amit he had felt so much like he was sitting in a living room with two friends that at one point he interrupted them, speaking out loud to a recording.
stories.insight: This is what podcast intimacy means: the listener feels part of a conversation rather than an audience at a broadcast. It is also why strangers approach Amit in public, which he welcomes as his greatest reward.
stories.quote: I felt so much that I'm sitting in a living room talking to two of my friends that at one point I interrupted you.

stories.topic: Fifteen Years of Friendship, One Podcast
stories.summary: Their friend Anjali Sharma told Ajay that she had known Josh Felman for fifteen years, yet his Seen and the Unseen episode revealed things that were completely new to her. Josh replied that she had simply never asked. Amit added his own experience: recording with friends of fifteen or twenty years, he realised mid-episode that he didn't really know them. Friendships skim the surface, and nobody asks about your parents or what makes you cry at night.
stories.insight: A long, attentive conversation opens a space that years of casual friendship never do. Much of what people would tell you, they are just waiting to be asked.
stories.quote: You never asked me, otherwise I would have always told you.

stories.topic: Ramachandra Guha in a Dark Room
stories.summary: Ramachandra Guha has been caricatured by both left and right, and has come on The Seen and the Unseen six times. In one conversation he described lying on his bed in a dark room listening to Hindustani classical music, losing all track of time, until his wife came home in the evening and found him there. The show notes link the exact ragas and performances, so listeners can hear what he heard.
stories.insight: A YouTube search on any expert turns up dozens of talks and panels, none of which shows you who the person is. Long-form audio can, and linking the music turns his anecdote into an experience the listener shares.
stories.quote: When you listen to them and you feel that thing and you know how he felt in that moment, that is a remarkable human connection.

stories.topic: Paul Simon on Poems vs Songs
stories.summary: Ajay recalled an interview in which Paul Simon was asked how writing poetry differs from writing songs. A poem, Simon said, is like a painting the mind goes over many times. A song is linear, so there is no second take. Attention is also uncontrolled: a driver ignoring the radio may get hooked midway by a sound or a phrase. So a good song can't require you to have been there from the start.
stories.insight: Audio, like song, is consumed in a line by distracted people. Don't build in prerequisites that only work if the listener caught every earlier moment.
stories.quote: Songs are linear. So you don't get a second take.

stories.summary: John Axon was a railway driver who realised his train was going out of control. He could jump and save himself, or stay on board and try to save lives further down the line. He stayed and died. A group of people wrote songs about him. They also went to his village and recorded interviews with people who knew him, train sounds, his family, even someone crying in the background, without planning to use any of it. Their masterstroke was putting all of it into the 1957 work.
stories.insight: This is 'show, don't tell' in audio. Hearing the people who knew a man talk about him says far more than a narrator announcing that his villagers thought well of him.
stories.quote: And then they had the master stroke that why don't we use all of this? And they used it.

stories.summary: A publisher offered to fly Amit to Delhi to record with Abhijit Banerjee in the same week he won the Nobel Prize. Amit asked for three hours; they offered one, and he declined. One hour would have meant talking only about the RCT work behind the prize. With three, he wanted to begin in 1963, when Banerjee's father taught Amit's father at Presidency College, Calcutta, and build a prehistory of the man.
stories.insight: The format decides what a conversation can reach. Knowing what you want lets you say no even to a celebrity guest, since fifty other people will happily do the one-hour version.
stories.quote: Like I don't care what kind of celebrity you are.

stories.topic: Five and a Half Hours, Book Never Mentioned
stories.summary: During a Bangalore trip with about six recordings in seven days, Amit stayed up all night writing several thousand words of notes on Sugata Srinivasaraju's massive new book on Deve Gowda. The next day they recorded for five and a half hours and never mentioned the book. Sugata's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched the city transform were fascinating enough on their own.
stories.insight: You don't prepare in order to show off what you know. Preparation gives you the freedom to follow a better conversation. Being his own boss, with no producer demanding 45 minutes on the book, let Amit go where nobody else goes.
stories.quote: The next day we met, we spoke for five and a half hours, we did not mention the book.

stories.summary: Amit admires Tyler Cowen, whose interviewing style is the opposite of his own: a list of brilliant prepared questions taken one after another without digressions. Cowen joined The Seen and the Unseen in a remote recording. Amit would ask a question, Cowen would answer crisply and stop, then the next question, and so on. Amit never found his usual flow. Neither of them was at fault; each was simply being himself.
stories.insight: There's no single right way to interview, but the host's and guest's styles have to mesh. Amit says he would approach a five-hour conversation with Cowen very differently today.
stories.quote: So it's a weird kind of like two opposite styles colliding.

stories.topic: Jerry Pinto Sends a Fan to Shanta Gokhale
stories.summary: At a book event in mid-April, Jerry Pinto and Shanta Gokhale were signing books in adjoining queues. A reader told Jerry that his eight-hour Seen and the Unseen episode had been transformational. Jerry answered by asking whether she had heard Amit's episode with Shanta. In his own episode, Amit and Jerry had teared up together while talking about their mothers.
stories.insight: Guests recommending one another's episodes is the strongest validation long-form work can get. It also shows that when a host is vulnerable, guests open up in return.
stories.quote: That is okay, but have you heard his episode with Shanta ji?

stories.summary: Amit asked Mrinal Pande his first question. She then spoke for more than an hour, in a mix of Hindi and English, while he said nothing. She took listeners from her childhood in the 1950s to the end of the 1970s: her parents, her mother, her sisters, her coming of age as a woman. Amit says a younger, callower version of himself might have cut in after two minutes.
stories.insight: Interruptions keep a conversation shallow, and silence lets people go deep. The magic came entirely from not stepping in.
stories.quote: And it would have been a disaster to interrupt at any point.

stories.summary: Before the Seen and the Unseen episode on the 1991 reforms, Amit worried that Shruti Rajagopalan, who is professorial and explains everything in detail, would dominate Ajay, whom Amit calls the crispest thinker he knows. The conversation went well. But Ajay kept getting thrown because Shruti narrated historical events in the present tense, and he couldn't tell whether she meant now or long ago.
stories.insight: Clarity includes tense. Ajay's rule is past tense for the past, present for the present and future for the future, which matters most when the listener can't rewind.
stories.quote: Because it's a modern American thing that events from history are narrated in present tense. And I just found it so confusing.

stories.summary: In Everything is Everything's Four Papers episode, Ajay talked about monetary and fiscal policy as easily as breathing, and Amit kept stopping him for lapsing into jargon. The released video is a cleaned-up version as a result. Amit's caveat is that this was the only time. Normally EIE is the organic conversation, only lightly cleaned up.
stories.insight: Experts can't see their own jargon. Part of a co-host's job is to speak up for the listener who is confused.
stories.quote: I was talking about monetary policy and fiscal policy, and for me these are just like breathing

stories.topic: Ali Abdaal's Thousandth Subscriber at Video Fifty
stories.summary: Amit points to YouTuber Ali Abdaal's subscriber graph, an exponential curve: a long flat stretch, then a line that turns almost vertical. Abdaal made two videos a week and only reached his thousandth subscriber around video fifty. His later advice to new creators: make two videos a week for two years and don't look at the numbers.
stories.insight: Exponential growth looks like failure for a long time. Someone who needs validation quits around video thirty. Someone who loves the work keeps iterating until they become good, and then great.
stories.quote: Now most people are not going to make fifty videos when they have less than a thousand subscribers.

stories.topic: Two Years Without Looking at the Numbers
stories.summary: When they started Everything is Everything, Amit asked Ajay not to look at the numbers for two years, about 104 episodes, and simply keep making the show. EIE is tiny next to The Seen and the Unseen, yet a loyal audience that turns up every Friday is already forming.
stories.insight: The hosts follow their own advice: during the early learning phase, keep the work separate from the metrics.
stories.quote: my plea to Ajay was let's not look at the numbers for two years.

stories.topic: The Fan Who Caught a Missing Show Note
stories.summary: Before he and Amit became friends, Sudhir Sarnobat listened to a Seen and the Unseen episode with around 114 show-note links. He wrote to Amit to point out one book that hadn't been linked.
stories.insight: People who love your work feel that they own a piece of it. An audience like that is worth more than any number of shallow likes.
stories.quote: And that is the kind of love that you want.

recommendations.item: Hardcore History
recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: Amit's first podcast as a listener, cited for his tip that one person is enough to tell a story.
recommendations.reason: Carlin reads about forty books per episode and then simply talks, with no sound effects and no dramatised delivery, and it is riveting. It proves you need neither a co-host nor production to tell a great audio story.

recommendations.item: Blueprint for Armageddon
recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: The roughly 26–27 hour Hardcore History series on World War One that first hooked Amit.
recommendations.reason: Carlin reads letters that soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a reckless mission in which they all died. That was the moment Amit understood the power of audio storytelling.

recommendations.item: The Ballad of John Axon
recommendations.context: A 1957 work, which Amit isn't sure whether to call a play or an album, about a railway driver who died staying on his runaway train.
recommendations.reason: A landmark in audio history. Interviews and background sound recorded in Axon's village went into the final piece, making it a masterclass in show, don't tell.

recommendations.item: Sun of the Family
recommendations.context: A Danish radio show from around 1997 about a young musician who killed himself. Amit asks listeners to post a link in the comments if it's available online.
recommendations.reason: The producers interviewed his parents, brother and girlfriend, and a whole person comes alive through the inflections in their voices and their particular memories. Amit calls it heartbreaking and a second landmark of show, don't tell.

recommendations.item: EconTalk
recommendations.creator: Russ Roberts
recommendations.context: Amit studied many podcasters' styles while building his course, and calls EconTalk legendary and the OG podcast.
recommendations.reason: It is the closest to his own approach: relaxed and conversational, with no fixed structure, going deep. It focuses on ideas rather than the guest's life.

recommendations.item: Conversations with Tyler
recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen
recommendations.context: Amit's example of the interviewing style opposite to his own.
recommendations.reason: Cowen asks great prepared questions, which Amit says someone like him couldn't even come up with, and moves through them crisply. It works beautifully and shows there is no single right way to interview.

recommendations.item: A Meditation on Form
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked when Amit urges podcasters not to be trapped by conventions about length.
recommendations.reason: It explains how form dictates content: what a five-minute conversation demands of a host compared with an eight-hour one.

recommendations.item: 1000 True Fans
recommendations.creator: Kevin Kelly
recommendations.context: Cited for the principle that it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many.
recommendations.reason: Kelly argued that creators don't need scale: a thousand true fans paying $100 a year comes to $100,000. It was theoretical when written, and Amit says subscription models like Substack have since made it real.

recommendations.item: 100 True Fans
recommendations.creator: Li Jin
recommendations.context: A recent follow-up to Kelly that Amit links.
recommendations.reason: It makes the same economics even more concentrated: a hundred fans paying $1,000 a year reach the same $100,000.

recommendations.item: Sinocism
recommendations.creator: Bill Bishop
recommendations.context: Amit's example of a creator who succeeds in a deep niche.
recommendations.reason: Bishop isn't a mainstream name, and he writes about China in a way so specialised that mainstream outlets might never commission him. Yet he is a superstar among his subscribers.

recommendations.item: How I Gained 1 MILLION Subscribers
recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Amit showed its subscriber graph on screen while discussing playing the long game.
recommendations.reason: The graph shows exponential growth: almost nothing for a long time, then a near-vertical line. His thousandth subscriber came around his fiftieth video.

recommendations.item: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Linked as the source of Abdaal's advice to new creators.
recommendations.reason: Make two videos a week for two years and don't look at the numbers. Amit calls this incredible advice and takes it seriously because it comes from someone who has done it.

recommendations.item: Furrows in a Field
recommendations.creator: Sugata Srinivasaraju
recommendations.context: Sugata's massive book on Deve Gowda, which Amit took thousands of words of notes on before their recording.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great book, even though their five-and-a-half-hour conversation never got to it.

recommendations.item: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (Episode 277, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Sugata Srinivasaraju
recommendations.context: The episode that never mentioned the book.
recommendations.reason: Five and a half hours on Sugata's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched his city transform, which is material no panel discussion about the book would produce.

recommendations.item: Playwright at the Centre
recommendations.creator: Shanta Gokhale
recommendations.context: Mentioned while describing his eight-and-a-half-hour episode with Gokhale, an authority on the subject.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great book on the history of Marathi theatre. Their conversation never even reached the subject.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Shanta Gokhale (Episode 311, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Shanta Gokhale
recommendations.context: One of the three eight-hour episodes Amit calls classics.
recommendations.reason: An eighty-three-year-old woman of many parts, given roughly one hour per decade of her life. Even Jerry Pinto points listeners to it.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Jerry Pinto
recommendations.context: An eight-hour episode that people still bring up to Amit.
recommendations.reason: Amit and Jerry teared up together while talking about their mothers. It is his example of how a host's vulnerability draws guests out of rehearsed sound bites.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (Episode 263, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Mrinal Pande
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a beautiful episode.
recommendations.reason: Her uninterrupted first answer of more than an hour covers almost thirty years of her life. It is his showcase for why a host must not interrupt.

recommendations.item: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (Episode 301, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Natasha Badhwar
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining how he structures long episodes around biography, work and ideas.
recommendations.reason: Amit's 'perfect episode' for construction, balancing all three with an extremely generous guest talking about parenting and writing.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Nilanjana Roy (Episode 284, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Nilanjana Roy
recommendations.context: Cited as the episode where he felt the balance went wrong.
recommendations.reason: Over 5 hours 45 minutes it leaned heavily on ideas and never reached her years in journalism. It still became a sleeper hit in his top ten by downloads, which shows his structural rules are guides rather than laws.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Ajay calls it the blockbuster eight-and-a-half-hour conversation.
recommendations.reason: People have told Ajay it is the single most perfect product for understanding the Indian state.

recommendations.item: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Josh Felman
recommendations.context: Raised by Ajay as an example of what a podcast conversation draws out of a guest.
recommendations.reason: It revealed things about Josh that even a friend of fifteen years had never heard.

recommendations.item: Episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Ramachandra Guha
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ramachandra Guha
recommendations.context: Guha has been on the show six times. The first two episodes were on Gandhi, and Amit read thirty books to prepare.
recommendations.reason: They show the person behind the caricatures, down to the ragas he listens to alone in a dark room, which are linked in the show notes.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Abhinandan Sekhri (Episode 254, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Abhinandan Sekhri
recommendations.context: Source of a listener compliment Amit treasures.
recommendations.reason: The listener felt he was sitting in a living room with two friends, so much so that he interrupted them.

recommendations.item: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: The first of Amit's four episodes with Karthik Muralidharan.
recommendations.reason: Three hours fifteen minutes transcribed to 45,000 words, about half a book. At double speed that is ninety minutes with an expert, which is why Amit sees audio as the most efficient way to go deep.

recommendations.item: A Scientist in the Kitchen (Episode 204, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Krish Ashok
recommendations.context: Linked alongside Amit's case for listening at higher speeds.
recommendations.reason: Krish Ashok shared the story of a blind colleague who listens at 6x, an example of how much the brain can adapt.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Shruti Rajagopalan & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while discussing Ajay's short answers as a guest.
recommendations.reason: It paired Shruti's professorial depth with Ajay's crispness. Amit feared a mismatch, but the three had a great conversation.

recommendations.item: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Episode 11, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked when Amit explains how he prepares for conversations.
recommendations.reason: Amit shares his screen to show how he researches a Seen and the Unseen episode: a list of themes prepared in depth, with no fixed order.

recommendations.item: 4 Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of the curse of knowledge being caught during recording.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls the released version a cleaned-up masterpiece because Amit kept stopping him whenever he slipped into economist jargon.

recommendations.item: Long As I Can See The Light
recommendations.creator: Chris Cornell
recommendations.context: Amit said he would talk 'as long as the light lasts' and Ajay quipped 'As long as you can see the light.' The show notes link Chris Cornell's version.
recommendations.reason: A musical wink that fits an episode literally recorded until the daylight ran out.

recommendations.item: ATR2100x microphone
recommendations.creator: Audio-Technica
recommendations.context: Amit's microphone recommendation for beginners.
recommendations.reason: It is a dynamic mic, so it picks up only what is close to it, which suits a home setup better than a studio condenser mic. It costs about ₹7,000 and has both USB and regular connections, so you can plug it into a laptop and also use it for Zoom calls.

recommendations.item: Anchor
recommendations.context: Part of Amit's point that everything you need to start is free.
recommendations.reason: Free hosting for your first episodes, which you can start recording on a mobile phone.

recommendations.item: Art of Podcasting: Brasstacks (notes PDF)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit had 10–11 slides on implementation but ran out of light, so he linked a document instead.
recommendations.reason: Covers the technical details of starting a podcast that he couldn't get through on camera.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: He has taught it to more than 2,600 people, and several of the episode's writing-for-audio tips come from it.
recommendations.reason: His full method for clear writing, including rules like putting the verb soon after the subject, avoiding 'the latter', and making every sentence go forward or deeper.

core_ideas.concept: Why Audio Can Go Long: When, How and Why We Listen
core_ideas.explanation: When: people listen while commuting, working out or doing chores, so they are a captive audience who won't switch tabs. How: many listen at higher speeds and lose no nuance. Why: most media is a mile wide and an inch deep, while audio is the most efficient way to go deep. Binge-watching shows that attention spans aren't the real problem. Ajay pushes back that only a small fraction of people crave depth and most want diversion, which is still enough to sustain a show. Amit replies that everyone has the capacity for depth and only needs a trigger.
core_ideas.quote: Attention spans are not the problem. When you want to go deep, you can go deep. And the most efficient way of going deep is audio.

core_ideas.concept: Try Higher Listening Speeds
core_ideas.explanation: The brain can comprehend up to about 500 words a minute, while people speak at 160–200. That spare capacity may be why we sometimes get bored listening to someone. Raise the speed in steps, to 1.2x and then 1.5x: each step starts to feel normal, until one stops feeling normal, and that is your natural level. The silences speed up too, so nuance survives. Don't judge anyone's speed. Ajay adds that this was a new discovery for him and is worth trying.
core_ideas.quote: And one should not be judgmental about what you listen at. What you listen at is what you listen at.

core_ideas.concept: Podcasting Is Not Time-Shifted Radio
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay first thought of podcasts as radio on demand. Amit says they are fundamentally different. In India, high FM licence fees push radio towards the lowest common denominator, and FM isn't even allowed to do news. Podcasting costs nothing but time, needs no licence, and allows both depth and intimacy. Because anyone can make anything, it uncovers niches nobody suspected existed, such as audiences for eight-hour conversations. Even a small niche in India, or across the world, is large in absolute numbers.
core_ideas.quote: And now you have a niche that nobody knew existed and the niche itself did not know it existed.

core_ideas.concept: A Voice in Your Head: The Distance Metaphor
core_ideas.explanation: Think about distance. Cinema is a big screen far away, filmed from far away, which suits westerns and car chases. Television is two or three metres away, which suits sitcoms. YouTube is half a metre away, with closer framing. Radio is like four people in a car, being broadcast to. A podcast is a voice inside your head. So you don't need a radio announcer's voice modulation, and putting one on would be a bug, not a feature, because listeners expect intimacy.
core_ideas.quote: Podcasting is a voice in your head. It is the most intimate medium in the world.

core_ideas.concept: The Two Imperatives: Respect the Listener, Be Yourself
core_ideas.explanation: Old media had the few talking down to the many. An intimate medium doesn't allow that, because listeners are accomplished people who often know more than you do, so respect their time and intelligence. Second, be authentic. When a student in his course asked what gap in the market he should fill, Amit said that thinking this way is a mistake. Among seven billion people and a million podcasts, the only thing that sets you apart is that you are you. Treat the show as your own journey, and people at any point on a similar journey will come along.
core_ideas.quote: There is only one gap in the market. You aren't there.

core_ideas.concept: Write for the Ear: One Thing at a Time
core_ideas.explanation: A reader can go back over a sentence; a listener washing dishes can't. So give one piece of information at a time. Don't put a dependent clause between the subject and the verb, as in 'Amit Varma, while...'. Avoid 'the latter' and passive constructions, which force the mind backward. When a story changes setting, signal the switch, and repeat who is speaking or where things are happening if needed. Repetition that would be bad in print can help in audio.
core_ideas.quote: So one thing at a time, and you kind of keep it simple, don't overload the listener

core_ideas.concept: Why Listeners Stay: Wanting and Structure
core_ideas.explanation: Don't be dogmatic about structure, but at every moment ask why the listener would keep listening. Usually it is empathy for a character plus curiosity about how their conflict resolves. Margaret Atwood warned that you can't take the reader for granted. Kurt Vonnegut said every character must want something, even if it is only a glass of water. Write the first draft as a brain dump, then restructure it with the listener in mind.
core_ideas.quote: Because what draws us into the story, it is that wanting, it is that desire.

core_ideas.concept: Show, Don't Tell: Verbs Over Adjectives
core_ideas.explanation: 'Show, don't tell' doesn't mean describing a scene. It means conveying something through action instead of abstraction: fewer adjectives, more verbs. The film cliché of the 'pet the dog' scene shows a character's warmth instead of announcing it, and words like 'nice' mean little anyway. In audio, you can show a person through the voices and memories of the people who knew them, as The Ballad of John Axon does.
core_ideas.quote: All of the action of the world, all of the interest in the world is in verbs.

core_ideas.concept: Forward or Deeper: Every Element Must Earn Its Place
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's rule for writing is that every sentence must either move the story forward or take it deeper, through context, detail or colour. The same goes for sound effects: footsteps on gravel can announce that someone is arriving, but effects added because they sound cool become intrusive. EIE learned this with on-screen inserts. They used to add too many; now there is no photo of Karl Marx just because his name comes up. Every extra element costs the audience some attention.
core_ideas.quote: Every element in any kind of story, audio or otherwise, must have a reason.

core_ideas.concept: The Curse of Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: When you know a subject well, you assume the audience shares your baseline. Crew member Vaishnav told Amit that a recent EIE episode skimmed over technical points he had wanted explained. In audio the listener can't go back, so introduce new voices quickly and set scenes clearly. In conversation, the host must keep one eye on the listener. Amit's technique is to say 'let me state this as I understand it' and restate the guest's point simply, so the guest can correct him if needed.
core_ideas.quote: The curse of knowledge is that when you know a subject so well, you imagine that the readers or the listeners will share a similar baseline of knowledge with it.

core_ideas.concept: Form Dictates Content, Content Shapes Character
core_ideas.explanation: Don't be trapped by conventions about length; Amit credits himself with shifting India's Overton window on how long a podcast can be. For a five-minute show you needn't read the guest's book. For half an hour, a ChatGPT summary will do. For an hour you must read the book. For eight hours you must read everything they've written, read around the subject and care about their life. First define your purpose: are you a fox or a hedgehog, interested in the subject or the person, their knowledge or their journey? Long form changes the host, because it teaches you to listen and to sink into another person's life.
core_ideas.quote: So the kind of form will dictate the kind of content. And the kind of content will dictate your character. It will change you.

core_ideas.concept: Take Guests Out of Autocomplete Mode
core_ideas.explanation: Authors arrive with prepared sound bites and can talk about their book on autopilot, like ChatGPT. Amit sincerely asks about their childhood and home, and makes himself vulnerable too. Guests then tend to open up in return. After they have talked about things they haven't discussed in forty years, they talk about their actual subject more naturally as well.
core_ideas.quote: And my task is to take them out of autocomplete mode.

core_ideas.concept: Over-Prepare, Then Let It Go
core_ideas.explanation: You will never know as much as your guest, but you need enough knowledge to follow their digressions. For his first episodes with Ramachandra Guha on Gandhi, Amit read thirty books. He usually ends up using only a fraction of his preparation, and that is fine, because it was never meant for showing off.
core_ideas.quote: And then I will find that I haven't used eighty percent of the prep that I have done, and it doesn't matter.

core_ideas.concept: Respect the Guest: Don't Interrupt, Listen to Understand
core_ideas.explanation: For Amit, not interrupting is an article of faith. Interruptions stop guests from going deep. Once guests expect them, they speak in half-sentences and can't make nuanced points. Most of us listen in order to reply or to look smart. Instead, put your ego aside and treat yourself as a bystander in the guest's story rather than its main character. Amit says this habit has made him more self-reflective and a better listener.
core_ideas.quote: Stephen Covey once said very wisely that most of us listen to respond, we don't listen to understand.

core_ideas.concept: Follow the Flow, Not the Question List
core_ideas.explanation: Panel moderators are often already thinking about question seven while the guest answers question six, and they miss the interesting digression in the answer. Amit prepares themes in depth but in no fixed order, and follows whatever thread comes up. Ajay notes this is a high bar. It separates real fluid intelligence from media that is about appearances and diction, because you have to understand what the guest said in real time and build on it.
core_ideas.quote: That path is where the magic lies. It is a road not taken by everybody else.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Scaffoldings of a Long Conversation
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's own theory for eight-hour episodes, which he is still developing. There are three overlapping frameworks: the guest's life story, their work, and the themes and ideas he wants to explore, many of which come up during the conversation. He moves between them in no fixed order and without breaking the flow. Too much on ideas feels abstract, and too much on life can also put listeners off. The Natasha Badhwar episode is his model of balance. The Nilanjana Roy episode leaned towards ideas but became a top-ten hit anyway.
core_ideas.quote: But the way I think about it structurally is I think of there being three overlapping scaffoldings.

core_ideas.concept: Bias for Action: Get It Done Over Getting It Right
core_ideas.explanation: In policy, Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe makes sense, but creators should do the opposite. The brain is wired to procrastinate, and you only learn by doing. Everyone is bad at first. Amit tells people to listen to The Seen and the Unseen in reverse order, and expects the hosts to see flaws in today's EIE episodes in two years. Vinay Sitapati once told him that perfection is the enemy of production.
core_ideas.quote: If you're faced with a choice of getting it right and getting it done, I want you to get it done.

core_ideas.concept: Life Is Not a Spectator Sport — Judge People by Their Best
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's motto since childhood is that playing cricket himself matters more than watching Sachin Tendulkar play. He argues that a culture which values people's best work and forgives their worst would lower everyone's fear of starting. Amit adds that creators should do instead of whining: if you don't like someone's work, make something better. And remove negative people from your life where you can.
core_ideas.quote: Then suddenly everybody's bar will come down and you know we'll be more ready to jump into the pond and do some things knowing that we suck and that's okay.

core_ideas.concept: Play the Long Game
core_ideas.explanation: Creators overestimate what they can achieve in the short term and underestimate the long term, because organic growth is exponential. If you chase the numbers and reshape your work around them, you lose your soul. If you make the work out of love, you keep improving through iteration. Ajay adds that putting on an inauthentic show can last only so long before you lose interest, while authenticity lets you keep going long enough to get better.
core_ideas.quote: creators also tend to overestimate the short term and underestimate the long term.

core_ideas.concept: Better to Be Loved by a Few Than Liked by Many
core_ideas.explanation: Amit credits the line to Paul Graham, as quoted by Sam Altman, and says he practised it long before he saw it put into words. People who love your work feel they own part of it and support it. Amit would rather have a hundred thousand people listen to an episode than get ten million YouTube likes. He contrasts many channels' average view time of about fifteen seconds with his own average listening session of about forty minutes. Kevin Kelly's and Li Jin's 'true fans' essays show the economics can work.
core_ideas.quote: It is better to be loved by a few than liked by many.

core_ideas.concept: Think Out of the Box — Including Language
core_ideas.explanation: When a show like Serial succeeds, everyone copies its structure, tone and voice; don't. In India, English-language podcasts are saturated with shows from around the world, while Hindi, Malayalam and other language audiences are underserved. If you can be authentic in another language, don't think of it as beneath you, because that audience needs you more and will love you more.
core_ideas.quote: So I would say if your proficiency in English is hundred and your proficiency in Hindi is eighty, do Hindi.

core_ideas.concept: Start Alone, Start Free
core_ideas.explanation: For storytelling, one person is enough. Dan Carlin proves it, and his first-ever episode would probably make him cringe today. Hosting is free and early episodes can be recorded on a phone. For a mic, choose a dynamic one over a condenser: studio condenser mics capture every nuance but also the room, while a dynamic mic, like the one a rock star holds at a concert, picks up only what is close to it. Imposter syndrome shouldn't stop you.
core_ideas.quote: the spoiler alert is that you can really do it for very cheap or you can do it for free.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's introduction: 'before Amit Varma became a world famous inventor and producer of a YouTube show, he in his previous incarnation pioneered the format of the podcast in India.' This is a gentle tease, given that EIE is tiny next to Amit's audio show.

To show what not to do in audio, Amit writes a sentence about his own arrest: 'The famous podcaster Amit Varma, while conducting a webinar on writing from his home office in Andheri, Mumbai, was arrested by the Delhi police for the crime of making Delhi more polluted by broadcasting his convoluted classes there.' The sequel: he 'protested his innocence before the officers in khaki, one of whom he berated for using an adverb.' The version rewritten for audio begins: 'The famous podcaster Amit Varma is behind bars.'

On why the verb should come straight after the subject: rather than 'Ajay Shah, while sipping from his herbal tea that he made with the seventy four herbs he had gathered in his garden...', Amit suggests 'Ajay Shah stabbed his co-host Amit with a knife', which he calls a much more dramatic way to put it.

Amit mimes jogging while describing a typical listener, Ajay smiles, and Amit demands, 'Why did you smile when I did this?' He drops the jogger for someone washing dishes. When he gestures again, the listener ends up 'washing dishes on an elevated platform.'
Defending the eight-and-a-half-hour episode with 83-year-old Shanta Gokhale: 'One hour for each decade of her life. Are you telling me that is sufficient?'

Amit's sign-off as the daylight fades: 'one piece of technology that you and I cannot control, Ajay Shah, even in these modern times, is the sun... the sun is kind of setting on us, but literally, not metaphorically, and not even literally because the sun isn't setting, the earth is turning.'

Amit's advice on his own back catalogue: he tells people to listen to The Seen and the Unseen in reverse order ('reverse order mein suno'), and not to watch the early episodes of Everything is Everything.

At the XKDR Forum anniversary party, Bhargav Zaveri asked guests to complete 'There are two kinds of people in the world...'. Amit's answer: 'the doers and the whiners.' On air he tells Ajay, 'And you have described the whiners.'
Amit promises to talk 'as long as the light lasts' and Ajay replies, 'As long as you can see the light.' The show notes link Chris Cornell's 'Long As I Can See The Light'.
Robert McKee, whom Amit describes as the author of many great books on storytelling: 'story is a natural form of thought.' Amit uses it to argue that audio is the oldest form of storytelling.

Margaret Atwood: 'A word after a word after a word is power.' Kurt Vonnegut: 'every character must want something, even if it is only a glass of water.' Amit pairs them on why you can never take the listener's attention for granted.
After Ajay's Paul Simon story, Amit's tribute: 'in the clearing stands a songwriter or a poet by his side', praising Simon as a remarkable songwriter and, in his own way, a great poet.
Neil Simon, from what Amit recalls as Barefoot in the Park: 'There are two kinds of people in the world, the watchers and the doers, and the watchers sit around watching the doers do.'
Abraham Lincoln's 'Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I'll spend the first five sharpening the axe', reversed for creators: 'You have to cut the tree to learn how to cut the tree.'
Asked whether he designs for loyal fans or occasional listeners, Amit says he doesn't think about the audience at all, quoting 'Ekla chalo re' (walk alone) and adding 'whoever comes comes along.'

Long-form company: Amit notes that Joe Rogan has done five-hour episodes and Lex Fridman at least one seven-hour episode. He also warns against Serial copycats that clone the same structure, tone and voice.
